mcqs.question: What does SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) mean in practice?
options: Each thread runs a completely different instruction stream in parallel
One instruction is fetched and decoded once, then issued to many threads that each apply it to their own data
A single thread processes multiple instructions per cycle using instruction-level parallelism
Multiple GPUs execute the same program on the same input
mcqs.explanation: SIMT's core saving is issuing one decoded instruction across many threads/lanes at once. Independent instruction streams per thread would defeat the control-logic savings SIMT provides; the other options describe unrelated mechanisms (ILP, multi-GPU).

mcqs.question: Why does a kernel launched with 33 threads typically cost close to double the resources of one with 32 threads?
options: Because the GPU rounds thread counts up to the next power of two
Because a warp (commonly 32 threads) is the real scheduling unit — 33 threads require a second warp that runs mostly idle
Because 33 is a prime number and primes are inefficient for GPUs
Because the extra thread must run on the CPU instead of the GPU
mcqs.explanation: Warps are the actual hardware granularity; any thread count that spills past a warp boundary consumes a full extra warp regardless of how few threads are active in it. There's no power-of-two rounding rule, no relevance to primality, and the extra thread still runs on the GPU.

mcqs.question: What actually happens when threads within one warp diverge on a branch?
options: The GPU spawns a second warp to handle the alternate path in parallel
The warp executes both paths sequentially, masking off threads not on the currently active path, so the costs of both paths add up
The divergent threads are dropped and their results are simply left undefined
The compiler detects divergence ahead of time and eliminates the branch entirely
mcqs.explanation: Divergence is handled by serializing paths within the same warp using masking, not by spawning new warps or dropping threads — this is precisely what erodes parallelism. Compilers cannot eliminate genuinely data-dependent branches.

mcqs.question: What is a key practical difference between SIMD and SIMT?
options: SIMD only exists in GPUs while SIMT only exists in CPUs

SIMD requires explicit vector-width packing by the programmer, while SIMT lets each thread look scalar and independent while hardware runs them in lockstep, incurring a divergence cost SIMD doesn't have in the same form
SIMT never supports branching of any kind, while SIMD supports arbitrary per-lane branches
SIMD and SIMT are simply two names for the identical hardware mechanism
mcqs.explanation: SIMD lives in CPU vector units and needs explicit vectorized code with no native per-lane branching; SIMT hides the lockstep grouping behind a scalar-looking thread model, which is exactly why divergence is a SIMT-specific concern. The other options invert or conflate the two.

mcqs.question: A GPU kernel has heavy per-thread branching where neighboring threads usually take different paths. What's the most direct consequence?
options: No consequence — GPU branch prediction handles this as cheaply as a CPU does
The kernel will fail to compile
Warps containing divergent threads serialize each distinct path, potentially collapsing much of the intended parallelism for those warps
The GPU automatically reorders threads across warps to eliminate the divergence
mcqs.explanation: GPUs lack per-core branch prediction the way CPUs do; divergence forces sequential execution of each path within a warp. The kernel still compiles, and GPUs don't automatically regroup threads across warps to avoid divergence — that regrouping has to be done by the programmer via data layout.
